tagline.text: A street festival in Legazpi each August, below Mayon Volcano, celebrating the Bicolano hero epic

location.label: Location
location.text: Legazpi City, Albay (around Legazpi Boulevard and Sawangan Park)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱7,000~9,000 (per person for 2 nights 3 days, excluding airfare and bus fare)

children.text: The Ibalong Festival honors Ibalong, the ancient heroic epic of the Bicol region, and is held in Legazpi each year around August as a non-religious festival. Its core is the street dance competition, a parade of costumed heroes and monsters, and the Mutya ng Ibalong pageant, and it pairs well with a trip to Mayon Volcano.

The Ibalong Festival is a cultural festival that Legazpi City in Albay holds each year around August. Unlike many Philippine festivals built around a saint or a religious event, it is a non-religious festival themed on the old Bicolano epic "Ibalong." The epic tells how three heroes, Baltog, Handyong and Bantong, in turn tamed a land overrun with monsters and made it fit for people to live in. At the festival, people dressed as these heroes and monsters march through the streets and reenact the old battles.

The festival was started in October 1992 by then-Mayor Imelda Roces. Its aim was to grow tourism and raise awareness of local history and culture, and the scholar Merito Espinas, who made the first English translation of the Ibalong, is said to have proposed the festival concept. Some scholars place the epic's setting around Magallanes in Sorsogon, so the Legazpi festival is closer to a celebration of Bicol culture as a whole than a historical reenactment. Only one manuscript of the epic survives, in Spanish, and local historians have interpreted it for later generations.

The schedule changes every year. It is reported to have run from August 21 to September 6 in 2025 and from August 7 to 23 in 2026, while the Tourism Promotions Board (TPB) festival calendar lists August 12-30, so sources disagree. Side events such as sports tournaments, exhibits, concerts and agri-trade fairs continue throughout the period, and the highlights are the street dance competition and the coronation of Mutya ng Ibalong (the festival queen) around the final weekend. Before fixing your travel dates, check that year's schedule with the Legazpi City tourism office or the festival's official Facebook page.

The festival area covers downtown Legazpi and the seafront Legazpi Boulevard. Bridges along the boulevard are named after the epic's three heroes, and the Baltog statue at the roughly 75 m Baltog Bridge faces Albay Gulf and Mayon Volcano. Sawangan Park lies along the boulevard and often serves as the stage for opening events and evening shows. Few areas charge admission during the festival, but some concerts or tournament seats may be charged separately, so check local announcements.

This is the most anticipated event of the festival. Schools and local groups compete in dance and costume on themes from the epic's heroes and monsters, and spectators line the parade route. It is reported to have been held on Saturday, August 22 in 2026, but the date changes every year.

Characters from the epic appear in large props and costumes, including Baltog, Handyong and Bantong, the serpent woman Oryol and the boar monster Rabot. Costumes use local materials such as abaca, rattan, coconut husk and shells.

This event selects the festival queen, and in the 2026 schedule the coronation took place on Friday, August 21. Together with the concert held right after the opening, it is one of the signature evening events of the festival period.

In 2026, an opening Mass was held at St. Raphael Parish on Friday, August 7, followed by a parade to Sawangan Park, then a concert and fireworks. It is a nice quirk that a non-religious festival begins in a church.

Boxing, billiards, darts, a Mayon bike challenge, golf, a dragon boat race and more are held around Legazpi. In 2025, boxing took place at Embarcadero de Legazpi and dragon boat racing on Legazpi Boulevard. Events and venues change every year.

The festival period features a battle of the bands, concerts, a cultural night, a food fair and an agri-trade fair, so you can taste Bicol food in one place. Lineups differ every year, and some events are announced late.

Between events you can take in the cone-shaped ridgeline of Mayon Volcano. Access zones are restricted depending on the volcano's alert level, so decide on any volcano tour after checking Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) announcements.

items.title: One Festival Day
items.subtitle: Mayon by day, festival by night

children.text: Aim for a clear morning view and look at Mayon Volcano from the Cagsawa Ruins in Daraga. Clouds usually start to build from late morning.
Move to Daraga Church and downtown Legazpi, have a late breakfast and leave your bags at your lodging.
Rest at your lodging or a mall to avoid the midday heat. Many days top
at noon.
Walk to Legazpi Boulevard to see the Baltog Bridge and statue, and enjoy the sea view at sunset.
Go to that day's venue (Sawangan Park or the City Hall area), find a spot and watch the show.
After the show, head back to your lodging by taxi or tricycle before the crowds build.
Event times and venues change every year, so this course is only an example. Check local announcements and reorder as needed.

items.title: Street Dance Day
items.subtitle: Claiming a spot early and watching the parade

children.text: Have an early breakfast and head to the parade route around City Hall. The route is closed to traffic, so walking is better.
Claim a viewing spot. The sun is strong, so bring a hat and water and look for shade.
Take photos as the costumed heroes and monsters pass. With many groups taking part, it can run for over an hour.
When the event ends, have a Bicol-style lunch at a restaurant downtown.
In the afternoon, rest or head to the nearby Cagsawa Ruins or a sunset view.
On days when the street dance competition is held, roads are closed and getting around is very inconvenient. Walk, or take a taxi from outside the closed zone.

items.title: Festival and Mayon in 2 Nights 3 Days
items.subtitle: An itinerary that combines the festival with Bicol sights

children.text: Fly in to Bicol International Airport in the morning, drop your bags at your Legazpi lodging, then see Legazpi Boulevard and the opening ceremony or an evening show.
See Mayon from the Cagsawa Ruins at dawn, tour nearby sights such as Daraga Church during the day, then go to a festival highlight event in the evening.
Have a relaxed breakfast, buy souvenirs and head to the airport. Book a flight in the afternoon or later to leave some slack.
There are direct flights from Manila (Ninoy Aquino International Airport) to Bicol International Airport (DRP), with a flight time of about
1 hour 20 minutes
. Cebu Pacific and PAL Express fly the Manila route.

Roads are blocked on parade and street dance days, so choose lodging within walking distance of the venue.

The Ibalong Festival runs over several weeks between August and early September each year, and the exact dates are set by City Hall. It ran August 21 to September 6 in 2025 and August 7 to 23 in 2026, so the start can shift by nearly two weeks. Announcements for the next year usually appear around June, so check then.

August brings midday heat together with sudden showers. Legazpi gets its heaviest rain from October to December and typhoons tend to cluster in autumn, so August is relatively manageable, but cloudy days are common and Mayon may be hidden.

For lodging, downtown Legazpi, the City Hall area, around SM City Legazpi and the Legazpi Boulevard side give good access to festival sites, and Daraga is an alternative. Rooms fill early during the festival and rates rise, so book as soon as your dates are set. Budget to mid-range hotels are reported at about
per night.

Be sure to try Bicol-style coconut milk dishes. Spicy Bicol Express and laing are the best-known examples, and the festival adds a food fair and more street stalls. Many stalls take cash only, so bring plenty of small bills.
Check that year's schedule and parade route with the Legazpi City tourism office or the festival's official Facebook page. Dates on calendar sites are often wrong.
On street dance day, arrive 1 to 2 hours early at the route to claim a spot.
The midday sun is strong, so bring sunscreen (SPF 50 or higher), a hat, water and a light rain jacket.
Carry a small crossbody bag to events and leave large backpacks at your lodging. Crowds make pickpockets a risk.
Prepare cash, mostly in small bills. ATMs can run out of cash early during the festival.
Book any Mayon Volcano tour for a different day than the festival highlights.
Hail taxis and Grab from outside the road closures, and for short distances walking is faster.
Book flights and lodging right after the schedule is announced.

Mayon is a volcano whose alert level changes. It was lowered to Alert Level 2 on August 5, 2026, and the 6 km Permanent Danger Zone stayed closed to entry, but it was reported raised back to Alert Level 3 after an explosive eruption on October 30. Always check the latest PHIVOLCS bulletin before any volcano tour.
Festival schedules differ between sources and change every year. Check official announcements before fixing dates.
Opening and highlight event dates change from year to year, and some events have been canceled over budget concerns.
On crowded days, watch for pickpockets and lost phones and keep valuables in front of your body.
Prepare for midday heat and sudden showers. Watch for heatstroke at outdoor events.
In heavy rain, lahar (volcanic mudflow) warnings may be issued for gullies around Mayon, so stay out of warned areas.

The remains of a church bell tower buried by the 1814 Mayon eruption, and a great place for photos with Mayon on a clear morning. It is in Daraga, close to downtown Legazpi, reachable by taxi or jeepney.
An old church on a hill with a view over the area. Being close to the airport, it is a good stop on your arrival or departure day.
